claims.text: Controlled grain refinement in single-phase high-entropy alloys can cause a transition from screw-dominated plasticity to edge-dislocation-mediated plasticity.
The dislocation-character transition increases yield strength and hardness until an optimal grain-boundary spacing is reached, after which further refinement causes softening.
The coarse-grained baseline alloy has a primarily screw-dislocation structure.
The coarse-grained baseline follows conventional Hall–Petch behavior.
Annealing and severe plastic deformation can be used to systematically refine grain size in the proposed alloy.
An inert atmosphere, quasi-static loading, and temperatures no higher than about 0.6 Tm avoid oxidation and significant phase or chemical-ordering changes.
Grain-boundary density and spacing govern the transition between screw- and edge-dislocation-mediated plasticity.
Increasing grain-boundary density near a critical spacing promotes the nucleation and mobility of edge dislocations.
Edge dislocations in these BCC high-entropy alloys are less temperature-sensitive than the conventional screw dislocations.
Edge dislocations are more effective than screw dislocations at impeding plastic flow.
Initial refinement produces Hall–Petch strengthening and hardening.
Below an optimal boundary spacing, dislocation multiplication can produce softening.
Below an optimal grain size, grain-boundary sliding can produce softening.
Relative to the coarse-grained baseline, initially grain-refined samples will have higher yield strength, higher hardness, and a higher edge-dislocation fraction.
Refinement below the optimal grain-size range will cause yield strength and hardness to plateau or decrease.
The proposed behavior is limited to single-phase refractory or similar BCC high-entropy alloys.
The governing transition occurs within a grain-size window in the tens-of-nanometers range.
The proposed behavior holds below approximately 60% of the melting temperature while the single phase remains stable.

contradictions.description: The prediction allows sufficiently refined samples to show a strength or hardness plateau or reduction, but the falsification rule treats failure to show an increase over the coarse baseline as falsifying the hypothesis without conditioning that rule on whether the samples lie above or below the proposed optimum.
